```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(yaml)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
claim   <- read_yaml("claim.yml")
# All columns as text: "[VERIFY]" and empty CSVs would otherwise change column types.
studies <- read_csv("studies.csv", col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
`%||%` <- function(a, b) if (is.null(a) || length(a) == 0) b else a
# Escape brackets that break markdown link text (kable already escapes "|").
md_text <- function(x) gsub("([][])", "\\\\\\1", x %||% "")
# Link only when the target is a real URL; "[VERIFY]" or a placeholder renders as plain text.
md_link <- function(text, url) {
  url <- url %||% ""
  ifelse(grepl("^https?://\\S+$", url) & !grepl("[", url, fixed = TRUE),
         paste0("[", text, "](", url, ")"), text)
}
# The study table gives each ID cell an anchor (id = study_id), so "S03" can link to "#S03".
row_links <- function(x) {
  ids <- trimws(strsplit(x %||% "", "[,;]")[[1]])
  paste0("[", ids, "](#", ids, ")", collapse = ", ")
}
# Front matter of another page as a list, or NULL if the file does not exist.
read_front <- function(qmd) {
  if (!file.exists(qmd)) return(NULL)
  l <- readLines(qmd, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  d <- which(trimws(l) == "---")
  if (length(d) < 2 || d[1] != 1) return(list())
  yaml.load(paste(l[(d[1] + 1):(d[2] - 1)], collapse = "\n")) %||% list()
}
```

for (v in claim$verdicts) {

               else sprintf("*Certainty: **%s**.* %s", v$certainty, v$certainty_note %||% "")

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**The 30-second version.** A tariff is a tax collected at the U.S. border on imported goods. In theory, who ultimately pays depends on whether foreign sellers cut their prices to stay competitive. Several independent studies of the 2018–2019 tariffs, using detailed customs and price data, found that foreign sellers mostly did not cut prices: U.S. import prices rose by roughly the full amount of the tariff, so the cost landed on U.S. importers, businesses, and consumers. Some of it showed up in store prices right away (washing machines are the clearest case); some was absorbed by U.S. firms' profit margins first. There is real disagreement about the size of the long-run effects on jobs and manufacturing, but not about who paid the tariff itself.
:::

## 1. What is the policy trying to address?

Tariffs are proposed for several distinct goals, and the "foreigners pay" claim matters differently for each: raising federal revenue without taxing Americans directly; protecting domestic manufacturing jobs from import competition; pressuring trading partners in negotiations; and reducing dependence on specific countries for strategic goods. This page tests only the first-order question of who bears the cost of the tariff. Claims about jobs, revenue, and national security are separate causal statements with their own evidence and belong on their own pages.

```{r related, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
# Optional (claim.yml related_claims): each related claim's current verdict and certainty,
# read from its own claim.yml. Missing or draft claims show as "not yet published".
if (length(claim$related_claims)) {
  cat("Related claims:\n\n")
  for (id in claim$related_claims) {
    other <- file.path("..", id, "claim.yml")
    page  <- file.path("..", id, "index.qmd")
    fm    <- read_front(page)
    if (!file.exists(other) || is.null(fm) || isTRUE(fm$draft)) {
      cat(sprintf("- %s — not yet published\n", id))
      next
    }
    rc <- read_yaml(other)
    grades <- vapply(rc$verdicts %||% list(), function(v)
      paste0(if (length(rc$verdicts) > 1) paste0(v$scope, ": ") else "", v$verdict %||% "",
             if (is.null(v$certainty)) "" else paste0(", ", v$certainty, " certainty")),
      character(1))
    cat(sprintf("- [%s](%s) — %s\n", rc$short_title %||% id, page, paste(grades, collapse = "; ")))
  }
  cat("\n")
}
```

## 2. What does economic theory say?

Theory does not settle this question; it tells us what to look for. A tariff drives a wedge between the price a foreign seller receives and the price a U.S. buyer pays. How that wedge is split is called *incidence*, and it depends on bargaining power. If the U.S. is a large enough buyer that foreign sellers will cut their prices to keep the market, foreigners absorb some of the tariff (economists call this the "terms-of-trade" effect). If foreign sellers can easily sell elsewhere, or if U.S. buyers have few substitutes, U.S. buyers absorb it.

- **Hypothesized effect.** Import prices rise by somewhere between 0% of the tariff (foreigners pay all of it) and 100% (Americans pay all of it). The empirical question is where on that line the 2018–19 and 2025–26 tariffs landed.
- **Trade-offs.** Even if Americans pay, tariffs can still achieve other goals: protection, revenue, or negotiating leverage. The cost is a reason to weigh those goals, not a reason they fail. This page does not grade them.
- **Unintended consequences.** Higher input costs for U.S. manufacturers that use imported parts; retaliation against U.S. exporters, farm goods especially; and supply chains rerouted through third countries.

Theory tells us which way to look, not how large the effect will be; that is an empirical question.

## 3. What does the empirical literature say?

The 2018–2019 tariffs were unusually well studied because they were large, sudden, and product-specific. That let researchers compare the prices of tariffed goods with similar untariffed goods, before and after. Every study below has a causal design; descriptive and opinion pieces were screened out (see Methods). Tiers reflect design quality and relevance under the protocol, not whether we agree with the finding.

```{r studytable, echo=FALSE}
studies |>
  mutate(Weight = paste0(quality_tier, ifelse(pub_status == "Working paper", "*", ""),
                         " / R", relevance_tier)) |>
  transmute(ID = paste0("[", study_id, "]{#", study_id, "}"),   # anchor for key-number links
            Study = md_link(md_text(citation), doi_or_url),
            Design = design,
            Setting = paste(country, period, sep = ", "),
            Outcome = md_text(outcome),
            Finding = md_text(finding_summary),
            Weight) |>
  kable(caption = "Included studies. Weight = quality tier A–D / relevance tier 1–3; * = working paper at time of review. Full extraction fields, effect sizes, and standard errors are in the downloadable CSV.")
```

[Download the full study table (CSV)](studies.csv) · [Search log](search-log.csv) · [Full-text exclusions with reasons](screening.csv)

**Direction.** Every study in the table finds that U.S. buyers, not foreign sellers, bore most or all of the 2018–19 tariffs [S01] [S02] [S03] [S04] [@amiti2019; @fajgelbaum2020; @cavallo2021; @flaaen2020]. **Magnitude.** Pass-through to U.S. import prices at the border was near-complete or complete [S01] [S02] [S03]. **Heterogeneity.** What happened after the border varied by product. Retailers initially absorbed much of the tariff in their margins rather than in shelf prices [S03], while washer and dryer prices rose quickly after the 2018 washing-machine tariff [S04]. **Mechanism.** Foreign sellers mostly did not cut their prices, so the terms-of-trade effect that would let foreigners share the cost did not appear in these data [S01] [S03]. The costs did not stop at the border: the aggregate real-income loss was small as a share of GDP but concentrated in farm counties hit by retaliation [S02]. **Gaps.** No study in this table covers the 2025–26 tariffs.

## 4. What can we conclude, and how sure are we?

**2018–19 tariffs.** The claim is not supported: U.S. buyers, not foreign sellers, paid nearly the entire cost of these tariffs [S01] [S02] [S03] [S04]. Our certainty is High. Below is how that grade was built; each row is a criterion from the protocol. All five criteria are proposed Strong for this generation: several independent teams using different data, agreement on direction, border estimates clustered near full pass-through, and peer-reviewed studies of the tariffs themselves. The grade describes the 2018–19 tariffs only and does not carry over to later rounds.

**2025–26 tariffs.** The claim cannot be graded for the newer tariff rounds. These tariffs are broader and larger than the 2018–19 round, and exporters may behave differently when most trading partners face tariffs at once, so the 2018–19 findings cannot simply be transferred. Section 6 says what evidence would let us grade this generation.

```{r certainty, echo=FALSE}
field <- function(rows, k) vapply(rows, function(r) as.character(r[[k]] %||% ""), character(1))
cs <- claim$certainty_scores
tibble(Scope = field(cs, "scope"), Criterion = field(cs, "criterion"),
       Score = field(cs, "score"), Why = md_text(field(cs, "reason"))) |>
  kable(caption = "Certainty criteria (protocol §11). Scored independently by two reviewers; disagreements noted in the Why column.")
```

```{r rationales, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat("::: {.callout-tip collapse=\"true\" title=\"Reviewer rationales\"}\n")
for (r in claim$reviewers) {
  if (nzchar(r$rationale %||% ""))   # the adversarial reader's comment is optional
    cat(sprintf("**%s (%s)** — %s\n\n", r$name %||% "", r$role %||% "", r$rationale))
}
cat(":::\n\n")
```

## 5. What is still unknown?

- **Whether very broad tariffs change exporter pricing.** The 2018 tariffs were targeted; tariffs covering most trading partners at once may give foreign sellers fewer places to redirect their goods, and no study here tests that.
- **How much of the cost absorbed in U.S. firms' margins eventually reaches consumers, and over what horizon.** Retail evidence covers the first months after imposition.
- **The long-run effect on domestic investment and plant openings.** Short event-study windows cannot capture it.
- **Distributional incidence.** Which households, by income and region, bear the largest share is not yet measured in the studies included here.

These are gaps in the evidence, not findings that the effects are small.

## 6. Where do experts disagree, and why?

Disagreement here is mostly not about the incidence finding. It is about what follows from it. Economists who favor tariffs generally accept that Americans paid for the 2018 round and argue that the cost is worth paying for strategic or industrial-policy reasons; that is a disagreement about **values** (which goals justify which costs), and it is outside the scope of this claim. A smaller group argues that pass-through estimates from 2018 overstate long-run incidence because supply chains had not yet adjusted; that is a disagreement about **time horizon**. Neither is a disagreement about the data.

**Steelman: “Foreign countries pay the cost of U.S. tariffs.”** The strongest version of the claim is that a buyer as large as the U.S. can force price cuts on exporters over time, and that currency depreciation abroad offsets part of the tariff for U.S. buyers. Evidence: [to be filled; currency-offset studies]. Checked by: *not yet checked by an adversarial reader (gate 6).*

**What would change our assessment.** Two or more peer-reviewed studies of the 2025–26 tariffs finding border pass-through well below 100% over a multi-year window, or evidence of sustained exporter price cuts in customs data.
